entries.title: Constraints that make developers faster
entries.summary: Ryan chats with Julien Verlaguet, CEO at Skip Labs, about finding the balance between human tolerance and tooling constraints, the spectrum of typed programming languages, and building cost-effective tooling for AI agents.
entries.content:
Ryan chats with Julien Verlaguet, CEO at Skip Labs, about finding the balance between human tolerance and tooling constraints, the spectrum of typed programming languages, and building cost-effective tooling for AI agents.

Skip Labs develops a programming language designed for reactive programming alongside specialized constraint-based tooling for AI agents.

entries.title: A look back before we look forward: A Developer Survey retrospective
entries.summary: This analysis compares the 2024 and 2025 Developer Survey data across three connected stories: the evolution of AI, humans at work, and demographics and community.
entries.content:
We are on the precipice of brand new results from the 2026 Developer Survey. We have 15 years of data and insights from this survey at our fingertips that shows more than just what one year’s collection of insights will explore. A year-over-year look at the Developer Survey offers the long view of what is changing in the broader technology ecosystem. This analysis compares the 2024 and 2025 Developer Survey data across three connected stories: the evolution of AI, humans at work, and demographics and community. The survey results reveal what the headline news cannot: how people actually fold these tools into daily work, where they still want human judgment, and how changing workflows affect the communities developers rely on.

The AI evolution from copilots to autonomous systems

AI tool usage has grown in our survey since we initially started asking about AI tools in the development workflow in 2023. 44% of developers indicated they were using AI tools in 2023, growing to 62% in 2024 and 79% in 2025, with almost half of all respondents indicating they used AI tools daily. What can the survey show us about this growth in AI usage that we don’t already know from news stories about frontier lab spending, AI stocks and earnings reports increasingly citing organizational restructuring enhanced with AI efficiencies?

We started asking about AI agents in the 2025 Developer Survey, with 31% of respondents indicating they were using them and most using ChatGPT (82%) and GitHub Copilot (68%). We held a smaller pulse survey in April 2026 asking about agents again, and this time we see agent use as almost doubled (59%) and Claude Code increasing in usage (from 41% to 55%). Something else the pulse survey on AI agents pointed out was that usage was driven by those that were daily users and those that were in more executive roles.

AI tools and their uses

When developers step into the world of AI tooling, ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot serve as the primary gateways. In our 2025 survey, 82% of those utilizing out-of-the-box assistants selected ChatGPT, while 68% turned to GitHub Copilot. Google Gemini trailed at 47%, followed by Claude Code at 41% and Microsoft Copilot at 31%. Farther down the long tail, niche offerings saw smaller footprints: Perplexity reached 16%, v0.dev hit 9%, Bolt.new gathered 7%, and Lovable.dev captured 6%. This breakdown suggests developers gravitate toward established platforms prior to experimenting with tailored autonomous setups.

Year-over-year trends reinforce this dynamic, even though survey design evolved. Back in 2024, when respondents marked single active usage options, 82% applied AI toward writing code, 68% relied on it for research, 57% tapped it for debugging, 40% drafted documentation, and 35% created general content. Because 2025 split these tasks between primary and secondary reliance, direct line-item comparisons are tricky. Nevertheless, the underlying trajectory stays clear: discovery and drafting lead the pack in automation, while actual software engineering remains predominantly assisted rather than autonomous.

Learning to use AI

Individuals who are learning to program are adopting automated tooling at an accelerated pace even as caution creeps in. In 2024, 63.0% of student respondents reported utilizing AI resources; by 2025, that metric climbed to 73.3%. This includes 39.5% engaging with these platforms daily, 18.7% weekly, and 15.1% monthly. This technology shift is part of everyone’s educational journey, with newcomers jumping in just as frequently as experienced professionals.

However, overall enthusiasm has noticeably tempered. Positive sentiment among learners dropped from 72.2% in 2024 (comprising 22.4% very favorable and 49.8% favorable) down to 52.8% in 2025 (19.3% very favorable, 33.5% favorable). Meanwhile, skepticism quadrupled, rising from 6.4% up to 26.3%. The overall survey population showed a similar cooling trend, moving from 72.0% positive and 6.4% negative in 2024 to 59.7% positive and 20.4% negative in 2025. Initial novelty is giving way to pragmatic evaluation as students confront inaccurate, incomplete, or confusing outputs.

Confidence in output accuracy similarly waned among students, with moderate or high trust sliding from 49.1% in 2024 (44.9% somewhat, 4.2% high) to 37.4% in 2025 (31.3% somewhat, 6.1% high). While 2025 introduced a neutral option that redistributed responses, the broader shift highlights a more discerning audience. Sentiments around handling intricate assignments echo this sentiment: favorable ratings for complex work fell from 41.5% in 2024 to 33.7% in 2025, while 18.6% admitted they avoid using AI for advanced tasks or remain unsure of its reliability.

Autonomous agents haven't quite won over the learning cohort, either. In 2025, 28.4% of students utilized agents, whereas 44.1% expressed no intention to implement them, compared to 37.9% across all survey takers. Concern over AI replacing jobs stayed flat at 15.0% across both years, though uncertainty dropped from 27.1% to 21.3% as unconcerned responses grew from 57.9% to 63.6%. Usage might be accelerating, but healthy skepticism remains, underscoring that using tools for study doesn't mean blindly embracing every feature on the horizon.

Work is about more than just a paycheck

Work-life balance continues to be an evolving story with the shifting office landscape. We have been tracking work setting in the Developer Survey since 2019 when only 12% of survey respondents indicated they worked fully remote. Since then, we saw a peak in remote work being reported in 2022 with 43% being fully remote. Hybrid work settings became the new majority for respondents in 2023 and 2024 at 42%. Last year we started capturing whether the hybrid situation was left up to choice, 13% indicated that their work situation was flexible enough for them to choose when to come into the office. We continue to ask about work setting this year and are curious about the implications it has with job satisfaction.

Job satisfaction is hard to pin on any distinct features because it is highly individualized. For early-career employees, work setting could be indicative of job satisfaction because they value learning from their peers and mentorship and hybrid or in-office is better suited for that. For people managers, work setting could be completely low stakes compared to what salary can provide in terms of job satisfaction. Some people may live in areas that make the experience of commuting to work enjoyable.

The 2025 survey data highlights how working environments have evolved past a basic split between remote and office settings into a much more nuanced picture. Across respondents, 32.4% reported working completely remotely, 17.9% stayed strictly on-site, and 37.1% navigated one of two structured hybrid models. Meanwhile, 12.6% noted high flexibility, coming in only when personal preference or project needs dictated. In comparison, 2024 figures stood at 38.0% remote, 42.0% hybrid, and 20.0% in person. Fully remote setups dipped roughly six percentage points year-over-year while strictly in-person arrangements edged down two points. Taking these updated granular options into account, total respondents enjoying some degree of remote work flexibility reached 82% in 2025, slightly above the 80% combined total recorded in 2024.

Geographic breakdowns give vital context to these top-level numbers. The United States led in fully remote participation at 45.0%, whereas India claimed the highest share of on-site professionals at 30.5%. European nations like Germany and the United Kingdom leaned heavily into flexible hybrid balances: Germany logged 20.7% in the flexible self-selected category alongside 24.6% in the flexible-leaning hybrid, while the UK registered 14.0% and 25.8%, respectively. France showed the strongest preference for office-leaning hybrid arrangements at 32.8%, well above the US metric of 16.7%. Tracking self-directed choice reveals key nuances that binary remote-versus-office surveys obscure: German tech workers maintained exceptional overall flexibility despite only 22.5% operating as fully remote.

Tools at work

Most engineers handle a structured yet manageable daily toolkit. Among the 27k+ individuals responding to 2025’s survey, 45.5% rely on 1–5 platforms while 35.4% utilize 6–10, showing that roughly 81% keep their ecosystem under ten primary solutions. An additional 9.5% work with 11–15 platforms, 5.1% use 16–20, and a final 3.8% operate across 21 or more systems. While widespread tool proliferation is rare, nearly one out of every five developers navigates over 10 systems to still cope with significant context-switching friction and maintenance overhead.

Foundational enterprise systems continue their steady expansion. Docker jumped from 35.0% in 2020 to 71.1% in 2025, Kubernetes scaled from 8.5% in 2019 up to 28.5% in 2025, Terraform moved from 6.2% in 2020 to 17.8% in 2025, and PostgreSQL surged from 32.9% in 2018 to 55.6% in 2025. Conversely, internal communication habits show shifting preferences: Microsoft Teams grew from 25.6% in 2020 to 53.1% in 2024, whereas Zoom dropped from 56.1% in 2022 down to 40.0% in 2024, and Slack adjusted from 53.0% in 2020 to 43.9% in 2024. Trello usage contracted from 29.6% down to 13.7%, while Jira remained remarkably consistent at 46.4% in 2025 compared to 47.7% in 2020; Confluence similarly held steady at 32.8% against 32.4%.

Next-generation, AI-focused developer tooling made its initial splash in enterprise environments during 2025. Cursor captured 17.9%, Claude Code reached 9.7%, Windsurf registered 4.9%, and Aider hit 1.9%; meanwhile, established mainstays like GitLab recorded 35.6% and Google Colab posted 7.0%. These early footprints don't reflect a fully-matured landscape just yet. Instead, they demonstrate that emerging AI offerings are quietly integrating alongside—rather than immediately displacing—the fundamental stack and collaboration layer powering modern tech organizations.

Job satisfaction in different countries

Overall job satisfaction presents a much more complex story than simple survey metrics might convey. For 2025, 28.4% of respondents reported feeling unhappy, 47.1% indicated feeling complacent, and 24.5% felt genuinely happy at work. The overwhelming majority resides in the middle ground, with nearly half of all developers feeling neither fully engaged nor actively disaffected. This signals that addressing career fulfillment is an ongoing opportunity for organizations, rather than a clear-cut binary of content versus discontented employees.

Regional variations highlight deeper trends. Tech workers in the US reported the highest happiness levels at 28.7%, with 27.0% unhappy and 44.4% feeling complacent. German respondents noted the lowest happiness rates at 19.2% alongside the highest share of complacency at 50.7%, whereas India saw the highest proportion of unhappy sentiment at 32.7%. UK figures landed at 31.5% unhappy, 46.4% complacent, and 22.1% happy; France recorded 27.4%, 48.0%, and 24.6%, respectively. While office policy alone doesn't dictate overall happiness, these figures demonstrate why global workplace strategies require local sensitivity.

Emerging AI shifts contribute to this changing dynamic. Developers identifying AI as a threat to their job increased from 12.1% in 2024 to 15.0% in 2025, while unconcerned responses dropped from 68.3% down to 63.6%, and uncertain sentiment ticked up from 19.6% to 21.3%. Concurrently, 2025 satisfaction factors place autonomy and trust to manage your own tasks at the very top, followed by competitive pay and benefits, solving real-world problems, and innovation through solving challenging and complex problems. Developers deeply prioritize independence and impactful projects precisely as automated systems introduce new questions around ownership.

Compensation shifts saw wide-ranging yet varied gains. Median annual compensation jumped 29.3% for product managers, 28.9% for applied scientists, 28.7% for game and graphics developers, 27.1% for mobile developers, and 24.0% for front-end engineers between 2024 and 2025. Conversely, growth was far more modest for data engineers at 5.1%, cloud infrastructure roles at 6.7%, and system administrators at 8.4%. Finally, the overall industry structure remains strongly grounded in hands-on technical roles: 85.3% identified as individual contributors compared to 14.7% in people management, reinforcing why professional autonomy and clear technical career ladders remain paramount to job satisfaction.

There’s learning to code, then there is learning to code for AI

AI is becoming part of how people learn to program, but growing use does not necessarily mean growing enthusiasm. Among Developer Survey respondents learning to code, 63.0% reported using AI tools in their development process in 2024, increasing to 73.3% in 2025. Over the same period, favorable sentiment toward those tools fell from 72.1% to 52.8%. These annual snapshots capture different respondents, but the contrast raises a useful question: how well does AI support understanding alongside getting something done?

The 2025 findings offer some context for that distinction. Among respondents answering the question about AI frustrations—not just those learning to code—20.0% reported becoming less confident in their own problem-solving, and 16.3% said it was hard to understand how or why the code worked. These responses do not establish that AI weakens learning, but they identify a difficulty worth investigating: producing working code and being able to explain it are now different processes.

Developers’ interest in learning from others provides another piece of the picture. In 2024, 41.0% of respondents answering how they used Stack Overflow selected learning technologies or techniques that were new to them, while 68.7% selected finding reliable guidance from community-vetted answers. In 2025, when asked to imagine a future where AI could perform most coding tasks, 61.3% of respondents said they would still seek another person’s help when they wanted to fully understand something, and 58.1% when they wanted to learn best practices.

Those questions measure different things—reported platform use and hypothetical preferences—but together they suggest a useful direction for future research. Beyond asking whether people use AI while learning to code, we need to understand what they learn from it: can they explain the result, evaluate alternatives, and apply that knowledge to the next unfamiliar problem? The retrospective establishes that AI use has become more common among learners. Whether that use translates into greater understanding remains an open question.

What to expect next

The broader trajectory does not suggest developers have blindly embraced or dismissed automated tools. Usage metrics keep expanding—climbing from 62% AI tool participation in 2024 up to 79% in 2025, with agent adoption surging from 31% in 2025 to 59% in the April 2026 pulse—yet enthusiasm is noticeably cooling. Favorable sentiment among students dropped from 72.2% down to 52.8%, while career anxiety rose from 12.1% to 15.0%. The next phase will be defined by how well tools, workplaces, and communities respond to that mixed reality: more AI in the workflow, more scrutiny of its limitations, and a continuing need for trustworthy human context.

The 2026 Developer Survey results can help us investigate some key questions:

  • Does the gap between AI use and favorable sentiment persist? Compare consistent measures and respondent groups, including people learning to code.
  • Does agent adoption come with greater delegation? Track frequency of use separately from the tasks and decisions people allow agents to handle.
  • How does control over work relate to satisfaction? Distinguish attendance arrangements from autonomy, and examine comparable groups before interpreting differences.
  • How does AI fit into community use? Separate visits for AI-related problems, demand for reliable guidance, participation, and belonging.

Be on the lookout for the results dropping here in the next few days.

entries.title: Organizations need decision-grade knowledge. AI makes it urgent.
entries.summary: AI can make the first part remarkably fast. It can find the page, the discussion and the person who might know. The harder work begins when those sources disagree, or when they become stale.
entries.content:
Imagine a customer asks whether your product supports their use case and how it handles their data.

You check the enablement page. It says yes. Someone in support remembers a newer conversation about a limitation. An engineer points out that the answer depends on the customer’s configuration.

You now have three relevant sources and a customer waiting for one answer. Who decides what the company can stand behind?

This happens in every organization. The question could concern a customer, an internal policy or a technical decision. Someone finds the documents. Someone else knows what changed. The group works out an answer, often in a meeting or a chat thread. A month later, another team starts the investigation again.

AI can make the first part remarkably fast. It can find the page, the discussion and the person who might know. The harder work begins when those sources disagree, or when they become stale.

Retrieval has become the starting point

A few years ago, finding the three relevant sources would have been a substantial achievement. Hundreds, if not thousands of products were built entirely around enterprise search, but the needs of customers have completely changed. Teams can connect their tools, search across them, and give a model relevant material to work with within minutes. Hybrid search, chunking, and reranking keep improving and these capabilities are increasingly accessible to teams building their own systems.

Now return to the customer. The enablement page may describe the original functionality. The support discussion may refer to a temporary limitation. The engineer may know a configuration condition that appears in neither source. Retrieving all three gives the team a better starting point but it does not establish which statement applies to this customer today. It does not give them decision-grade knowledge.

This is where many AI experiences lose people. An answer appears quickly and sounds complete. The person receiving it still has to check the sources, find the missing condition and ask a colleague to confirm it. They are doing the last and most consequential part of the work themselves.

That fatigue is reasonable. If an organization wants people to use AI for consequential questions, it has to give them a way to assess the knowledge behind the response.

What the answer needs to carry

For a business-critical question, you need five things before relying on an answer.

  • Where did it come from? I need the underlying sources and enough provenance to inspect them.
  • When and where does it apply? A correct answer for one product version, region, or customer configuration may be wrong for another.
  • Am I allowed to use it? Knowledge must respect the permissions of its sources and the boundaries the organization sets.
  • Does anything disagree? If a newer discussion contradicts an older page, the system should help bring that disagreement into view.
  • Who can resolve it? Sometimes the answer requires a person who owns the capability or understands the exception.

This is what I mean by decision-grade knowledge. People and agents need evidence, context, and a way to improve the knowledge when it changes. Each part affects whether an answer can support a decision.

A citation alone cannot tell the customer which guidance applies. A trust score cannot take responsibility for a product commitment. Both can help the team investigate, but the judgment of people who understand the work still matters.

Put human expertise where it counts

In our example, product can confirm the current capability. Engineering can explain the configuration. Support can tell us what customers are encountering. Each person contributes something the sources alone may miss.

But let’s also be honest here; we do not want those people reviewing every response an AI tool produces. That would create another queue and pull experts away from their work. I want their expertise brought in when a consequential answer is uncertain, when sources conflict or when knowledge used by many people needs validation.

Their contribution also needs to last. Once the team resolves the customer question, the result should include the answer, the conditions under which it applies and the evidence behind it. If something changes, a person should be able to correct it. The next team should start with that work already done.

AI has a useful role throughout this process. It can retrieve and compare sources, help identify gaps, and make validated knowledge available in the next workflow. People establish meaning and resolve the cases where the organization has yet to reach an answer. That is how we want humans and AI to work together on knowledge.

Why we built Stack Internal this way

Stack Overflow has spent nearly two decades learning what happens when people share expertise in a form others can find, examine, and improve. An answer is useful. A correction makes it more useful. The history of that work helps the next person assess what they have found. Stack Internal Community brought those practices inside organizations.

Today we are opening the Stack Internal platform to more people and teams. We are bringing knowledge from an organization’s sources into a shared layer, preserving the context needed to use it responsibly, and making it available through chat, API, and MCP. Subject matter experts have a role in validating and correcting knowledge that others depend on. That role is intentional and is respectful of their time and effort.

The same customer question may come from a person using chat, an internal application using the API, or an agent using MCP. The organization needs a consistent basis for the answer across those experiences. The interface can change. The sources, access rules, and human contributions need to be carried through.

Our companion launch post covers the full capabilities available today and how to get started. I wanted to explain the product decision behind them: we are building for the point where an organization has to decide what it knows, who can use it, and how that knowledge changes.

The next question we are working on

The team resolves the customer question. Product confirms the functionality, engineering explains the configuration, and support identifies the exception. Six months later, the functionality changes.

We need the earlier answer to be correctable. We also need a better way to keep what the team learned in the first place.

Think about how often useful knowledge is created in a one-to-one conversation. Someone works through a difficult question with a colleague or an AI agent. They compare sources, discover an exception, and reach a conclusion. The session ends. That conclusion may never become available to anyone else.

We are already working on ways for people and agents to push useful knowledge back into Stack Internal through the tools where they work. The person contributing it should be able to decide what is worth keeping and who can access it. An expert’s correction should remain connected to the guidance it corrects. Over time, we want the system to help turn resolved conversations into reusable knowledge, identify when sources conflict, and bring the right person in when an answer needs attention.

Knowledge flows to a person or agent when they need it. What they learn can flow back, with evidence, ownership, and appropriate access. The next answer starts from the work already done.

Eventually, we want Stack Internal to help before someone knows which question to ask. It should surface a relevant decision, an unresolved conflict, or a gap that could affect the work in front of them. We have a lot to prove and build before we reach that point and will share more as we go.

Our goal is organizations where a hard-won answer does not disappear with the meeting, chat thread, or AI session that produced it. Each decision and correction should make the next one easier.

entries.title: Anyone can start building verified knowledge with Stack Internal
entries.summary: Stack Internal transforms your daily work into a living memory that’s shared with the rest of your team. Now anyone can create and share their knowledge in a Stack Internal workspace for free by visiting stackinternal.com.
entries.content:
While most platforms stick to storing or retrieving your content, Stack Internal helps you and your AI agents make higher quality decisions by delivering knowledge that is context-aware, vetted by experts, and grounded in traceable evidence. We’ve built Stack Internal using the core curation mechanism that Stack Overflow has been scaling for nearly two decades. Now, we’ve built upon that foundation and enhanced it to fit an AI-first world, putting that trusted mechanism directly into the tools and AI agents your teams already use. Your organization won’t forget what it knows. With Stack Internal, your organization’s memory is always learning and improving so the next person, team, or agent gets decision-grade knowledge.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Stack Internal. Now anyone can create and share their knowledge in a Stack Internal workspace for free by visiting stackinternal.com.

What’s new

In July, we introduced the Stack Internal platform to existing customers, giving them new ways to use their Stack Internal Community knowledge through Chat, API, and MCP. On September 30, we are opening the platform to more people: anyone can create a free Starter workspace, while organizations gain new options for bringing in knowledge from their own systems and governing how it is used. This release also expands source coverage and adds tools for expert validation, permissions, and usage visibility. Below is what is available and how to get started.

What you can do

Create a free workspace

Anyone can get started with Stack Internal by creating a Starter workspace. It’s a free way to connect to your top three data sources, capture and store verified knowledge from those sources, and even collaborate with a couple of teammates. Start transforming your daily work into living memory. See what plan works best for you.

Bring data in from anywhere

We have expanded our integrations to safely bring more of your knowledge into your workspace. Ingest critical context persistently from our out-of-the-box connectors. The new Microsoft Teams connector captures learnings from standard, private, and shared channels. And our Slack and Google Docs connectors now respect source permissions, allowing you to ingest restricted and private content securely. With this release, you can ingest knowledge from any source or tool your team uses via our new ingestion API. From wikis, repos, and ticketing tools, we’ve got you covered.

Inspect traceable evidence

Stack Internal evaluates knowledge using signals such as provenance, recency, expertise, corroboration, and human validation. For AI agents, those signals can be translated into a machine-facing trust score so they pull the best answers. The system also automatically flags conflicting information at response time, converting team know-how into validated institutional knowledge.

Get expert validation

It also automatically detects Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) based on topics. When a critical knowledge gap arises, users and AI agents can trigger an SME validation workflow that notifies the right expert directly in Slack. SMEs can then confirm or update answers in Slack, or they can manage these validation requests through the platform interface.

Deliver trusted knowledge anywhere

With our MCP Server, you can push trusted, Stack Internal knowledge into Claude, Codex, Cursor, or any other tool or agent your team uses. The code, answers, or solutions are grounded in your organization’s verified know-how, not just what a model guessed.

Access enterprise governance

Establishing trust requires robust governance, so we’re introducing custom roles and permissions. Administrators can appoint knowledge managers and reporting analysts, while managing who can view audit log data or delete content. We have added full activity tracking and self-serve exportable audit trails to provide clear source provenance for every agent decision. To track platform engagement, a new knowledge health and usage dashboard lets you view metrics like Helpful Answer Rate and Daily Active Users.

Activate your community knowledge

In our recent Stack Internal Community 2026.6 release, we laid a stronger foundation for enterprise trust by delivering centralized admin security controls, including header-enforced API keys, configurable rate limits, and automated lifecycle tools like article expiration to prevent knowledge decay. Building on this momentum, our September 30 release (2026.7) unlocks even richer administrative control and API functionality across your community instance. On the API front, 2026.7 introduces new v3 endpoints for aggregate reputation leaderboards, badge catalog discovery, and user activity filtering for answers and comments, alongside a scoped content-import API that enables seamless migration of questions, answers, and articles with full author attribution.

What’s next

Today, Stack Internal brings knowledge from the places your team works into the tools where people and agents need it. We are building the other half of that cycle too: a way to improve your organization’s knowledge flywheel, so what people learn while working is accessible for the rest of the organization to use.

Imagine an engineer working in their IDE and finding a fix to a problem that does not yet exist in your knowledge layer. That knowledge should not disappear when the chat or AI session ends. People should be able to bring it back into Stack Internal effortlessly, preserve the evidence behind it, and decide who can use it, so that the next person or agent that runs into this problem has decision-grade knowledge within seconds.

We are also building 'Scopes' to make those contextual boundaries more useful. You might keep working knowledge in an individual space, share a decision with your project team, then make approved guidance available across the organization. Each step should be intentional, with clear control over who can see the knowledge and which people or agents can use it. The same principle applies when a team’s information needs to stay within that team.

Over time, we want Stack Internal to make aging knowledge and conflicting sources easier to spot, involve the right experts, and surface relevant knowledge before someone thinks to search. The platform already helps bring knowledge in and deliver it where it is needed. We are building toward a system that learns from the people and agents using it.

Stay tuned. We can't wait to show you what we've built.

Ready to try Stack Internal? Create a free workspace and start with the knowledge your team already has.

Already a Stack Internal customer? Sign in to your workspace or contact your account team about enabling the platform. Check out the guide here.

entries.title: Getting ready for 2026 results: A look back on Developer Survey findings

Usage might be accelerating, but healthy skepticism remains, underscoring that using tools for study doesn't mean blindly embracing every feature on the horizon.

Work is about more than just a paycheck

Work-life balance continues to be an evolving story with the shifting office landscape. We have been tracking work setting in the Developer Survey since 2019 when only 12% of survey respondents indicated they worked fully remote. Since then, we saw a peak in remote work being reported in 2022 with 43% being fully remote. Hybrid work settings became the new majority for respondents in 2023 and 2024 at 42%. Last year we started capturing whether the hybrid situation was left up to choice, 13% indicated that their work situation was flexible enough for them to choose when to come into the office. We continue to ask about work setting this year and are curious about the implications it has with job satisfaction.

Job satisfaction is hard to pin on any distinct features because it is highly individualized. For early-career employees, work setting could be indicative of job satisfaction because they value learning from their peers and mentorship and hybrid or in-office is better suited for that. For people managers, work setting could be completely low stakes compared to what salary can provide in terms of job satisfaction. Some people may live in areas that make the experience of commuting to work enjoyable.

The 2025 survey data highlights how working environments have evolved past a basic split between remote and office settings into a much more nuanced picture. Across respondents, 32.4% reported working completely remotely, 17.9% stayed strictly on-site, and 37.1% navigated one of two structured hybrid models. Meanwhile, 12.6% noted high flexibility, coming in only when personal preference or project needs dictated. In comparison, 2024 figures stood at 38.0% remote, 42.0% hybrid, and 20.0% in person. Fully remote setups dipped roughly six percentage points year-over-year while strictly in-person arrangements edged down two points. Taking these updated granular options into account, total respondents enjoying some degree of remote work flexibility reached 82% in 2025, slightly above the 80% combined total recorded in 2024.

Geographic breakdowns give vital context to these top-level numbers. The United States led in fully remote participation at 45.0%, whereas India claimed the highest share of on-site professionals at 30.5%. European nations like Germany and the United Kingdom leaned heavily into flexible hybrid balances: Germany logged 20.7% in the flexible self-selected category alongside 24.6% in the flexible-leaning hybrid, while the UK registered 14.0% and 25.8%, respectively. France showed the strongest preference for office-leaning hybrid arrangements at 32.8%, well above the US metric of 16.7%. Tracking self-directed choice reveals key nuances that binary remote-versus-office surveys obscure: German tech workers maintained exceptional overall flexibility despite only 22.5% operating as fully remote.

Tools at work

Most engineers handle a structured yet manageable daily toolkit. Among the 27k+ individuals responding to 2025’s survey, 45.5% rely on 1–5 platforms while 35.4% utilize 6–10, showing that roughly 81% keep their ecosystem under ten primary solutions. An additional 9.5% work with 11–15 platforms, 5.1% use 16–20, and a final 3.8% operate across 21 or more systems. While widespread tool proliferation is rare, nearly one out of every five developers navigates over 10 systems to still cope with significant context-switching friction and maintenance overhead.

Foundational enterprise systems continue their steady expansion. Docker jumped from 35.0% in 2020 to 71.1% in 2025, Kubernetes scaled from 8.5% in 2019 up to 28.5% in 2025, Terraform moved from 6.2% in 2020 to 17.8% in 2025, and PostgreSQL surged from 32.9% in 2018 to 55.6% in 2025. Conversely, internal communication habits show shifting preferences: Microsoft Teams grew from 25.6% in 2020 to 53.1% in 2024, whereas Zoom dropped from 56.1% in 2022 down to 40.0% in 2024, and Slack adjusted from 53.0% in 2020 to 43.9% in 2024. Trello usage contracted from 29.6% down to 13.7%, while Jira remained remarkably consistent at 46.4% in 2025 compared to 47.7% in 2020; Confluence similarly held steady at 32.8% against 32.4%.

Next-generation, AI-focused developer tooling made its initial splash in enterprise environments during 2025. Cursor captured 17.9%, Claude Code reached 9.7%, Windsurf registered 4.9%, and Aider hit 1.9%; meanwhile, established mainstays like GitLab recorded 35.6% and Google Colab posted 7.0%. These early footprints don't reflect a fully-matured landscape just yet. Instead, they demonstrate that emerging AI offerings are quietly integrating alongside—rather than immediately displacing—the fundamental stack and collaboration layer powering modern tech organizations.

Job satisfaction in different countries

Overall job satisfaction presents a much more complex story than simple survey metrics might convey. For 2025, 28.4% of respondents reported feeling unhappy, 47.1% indicated feeling complacent, and 24.5% felt genuinely happy at work. The overwhelming majority resides in the middle ground, with nearly half of all developers feeling neither fully engaged nor actively disaffected. This signals that addressing career fulfillment is an ongoing opportunity for organizations, rather than a clear-cut binary of content versus discontented employees.

Regional variations highlight deeper trends. Tech workers in the US reported the highest happiness levels at 28.7%, with 27.0% unhappy and 44.4% feeling complacent. German respondents noted the lowest happiness rates at 19.2% alongside the highest share of complacency at 50.7%, whereas India saw the highest proportion of unhappy sentiment at 32.7%. UK figures landed at 31.5% unhappy, 46.4% complacent, and 22.1% happy; France recorded 27.4%, 48.0%, and 24.6%, respectively. While office policy alone doesn't dictate overall happiness, these figures demonstrate why global workplace strategies require local sensitivity.

Emerging AI shifts contribute to this changing dynamic. Developers identifying AI as a threat to their job increased from 12.1% in 2024 to 15.0% in 2025, while unconcerned responses dropped from 68.3% down to 63.6%, and uncertain sentiment ticked up from 19.6% to 21.3%. Concurrently, 2025 satisfaction factors place autonomy and trust to manage your own tasks at the very top, followed by competitive pay and benefits, solving real-world problems, and innovation through solving challenging and complex problems. Developers deeply prioritize independence and impactful projects precisely as automated systems introduce new questions around ownership.

Compensation shifts saw wide-ranging yet varied gains. Median annual compensation jumped 29.3% for product managers, 28.9% for applied scientists, 28.7% for game and graphics developers, 27.1% for mobile developers, and 24.0% for front-end engineers between 2024 and 2025. Conversely, growth was far more modest for data engineers at 5.1%, cloud infrastructure roles at 6.7%, and system administrators at 8.4%. Finally, the overall industry structure remains strongly grounded in hands-on technical roles: 85.3% identified as individual contributors compared to 14.7% in people management, reinforcing why professional autonomy and clear technical career ladders remain paramount to job satisfaction.

There’s learning to code, then there is learning to code for AI

AI is becoming part of how people learn to program, but growing use does not necessarily mean growing enthusiasm. Among Developer Survey respondents learning to code, 63.0% reported using AI tools in their development process in 2024, increasing to 73.3% in 2025. Over the same period, favorable sentiment toward those tools fell from 72.1% to 52.8%. These annual snapshots capture different respondents, but the contrast raises a useful question: how well does AI support understanding alongside getting something done?

The 2025 findings offer some context for that distinction. Among respondents answering the question about AI frustrations—not just those learning to code—20.0% reported becoming less confident in their own problem-solving, and 16.3% said it was hard to understand how or why the code worked. These responses do not establish that AI weakens learning, but they identify a difficulty worth investigating: producing working code and being able to explain it are now different processes.

Developers’ interest in learning from others provides another piece of the picture. In 2024, 41.0% of respondents answering how they used Stack Overflow selected learning technologies or techniques that were new to them, while 68.7% selected finding reliable guidance from community-vetted answers. In 2025, when asked to imagine a future where AI could perform most coding tasks, 61.3% of respondents said they would still seek another person’s help when they wanted to fully understand something, and 58.1% when they wanted to learn best practices.

Those questions measure different things—reported platform use and hypothetical preferences—but together they suggest a useful direction for future research. Beyond asking whether people use AI while learning to code, we need to understand what they learn from it: can they explain the result, evaluate alternatives, and apply that knowledge to the next unfamiliar problem? The retrospective establishes that AI use has become more common among learners. Whether that use translates into greater understanding remains an open question.

What to expect next

The broader trajectory does not suggest developers have blindly embraced or dismissed automated tools. Usage metrics keep expanding—climbing from 62% AI tool participation in 2024 up to 79% in 2025, with agent adoption surging from 31% in 2025 to 59% in the April 2026 pulse—yet enthusiasm is noticeably cooling. Favorable sentiment among students dropped from 72.2% down to 52.8%, while career anxiety rose from 12.1% to 15.0%. The next phase will be defined by how well tools, workplaces, and communities respond to that mixed reality: more AI in the workflow, more scrutiny of its limitations, and a continuing need for trustworthy human context.

The 2026 Developer Survey results can help us investigate some key questions:

  • Does the gap between AI use and favorable sentiment persist? Compare consistent measures and respondent groups, including people learning to code.
  • Does agent adoption come with greater delegation? Track frequency of use separately from the tasks and decisions people allow agents to handle.
  • How does control over work relate to satisfaction? Distinguish attendance arrangements from autonomy, and examine comparable groups before interpreting differences.
  • How does AI fit into community use? Separate visits for AI-related problems, demand for reliable guidance, participation, and belonging.

Be on the lookout for the results dropping here in the next days.
